warning: There is NO official conversion from a national grade to a US 4.0 GPA. The us_letter_convention and us_gpa_convention columns record the mapping US admissions offices commonly apply; credential evaluators publish tables that disagree, most sharply at the top of each scale. The local classification is the reliable field — it is what the transcript states.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.notes: Argentine universities mark out of 10, but the pass mark varies: 4 at most public universities, 6 at some private ones. The transcript legend is the authority.

countries.name: Australia
countries.notes: The letters are a trap for a US reader: an Australian D is a Distinction, the second-highest grade, not the near-fail a D means in the United States. Bands vary a few points between universities.

countries.name: Austria
countries.notes: Austria uses whole numbers 1 to 5 with 1 as the best grade and 5 as a failure — the same direction as Germany but with five bands rather than a decimal scale.

countries.name: Bangladesh
countries.notes: Bangladeshi universities already grade on a 4.0 scale, so the number transfers almost directly. It is not identical: the bands beneath it are stricter, so a Bangladeshi 3.5 represents stronger work than a US 3.5 usually does.

countries.name: Belgium

bands.local: La plus grande distinction / Grootste onderscheiding

countries.notes: Belgium marks out of 20 like France, with named distinctions rather than mentions. The distinctions are the part a US admissions office can read directly.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.notes: Brazilian universities set their own pass mark, usually 6 or 7 out of 10 — the transcript legend states which. Some issue a Conceito (A/B/C/D) instead of a number.

countries.name: Canada
countries.notes: Canada has no national scale. Provinces and individual universities differ by several points at every boundary, and some use a 9-point or 12-point letter scale instead of percentages. Check the legend printed on the back of the transcript before trusting any conversion.

countries.name: Chile
countries.notes: The Chilean scale runs 1 to 7 with 4 as the pass mark, so the usable range is narrow and a 5.5 is a genuinely good result.

countries.name: China
countries.notes: The pass mark is 60, not 50, and the practical ceiling is lower than a US reader expects — a 90 average is genuinely exceptional. Chinese universities issue their own 4.0 conversion on the transcript far more often than European ones do; where that appears, use it.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.notes: Colombia marks out of 5.0 and passes at 3.0. A Colombian 4.0 is a strong result near the top of the scale, not the perfect score the same number means in the US.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.notes: Czech grades run 1 to 4 with 1 as the best, the same direction as Germany. Only three passing grades exist, so the scale carries less information than a US GPA does.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.notes: The Danish scale has seven steps with gaps in the numbering — 12, 10, 7, 4, 02, 00, -3 — and no grade between them. A negative grade is a real mark, not a data error.

countries.name: Egypt
countries.notes: Egyptian marking is severe: an Excellent starts at 85 and is rare, and a Good at 65 represents solid work rather than the mediocrity the number suggests to a US reader.

countries.name: Finland
countries.notes: Finnish universities grade 1 to 5 with 0 as a fail. Some courses are pass/fail only, which carries no GPA information.

countries.name: France
countries.notes: French marking is famously severe at the top: 20/20 is essentially never awarded and a 16 is an outstanding result. Scaling a French grade proportionally — treating 14/20 as 70% — understates it badly, which is why the mention (très bien, bien) carries the meaning.

countries.name: Germany
countries.notes: The German scale runs backwards: 1.0 is the best grade and 4.0 is the lowest pass. A German 1.3 is an excellent degree, not a failing one. German universities also apply the modified Bavarian formula when converting inbound grades, which is a different calculation again.

countries.name: Ghana
countries.notes: Ghanaian universities grade on a 4.0 CGPA, so the number transfers with little change, and add a British-style honours class.

countries.name: Greece
countries.notes: Greek degree classes are broad — Λίαν Καλώς covers a two-point span — so the underlying number matters more here than the class name does.

countries.name: Hong Kong
countries.notes: Hong Kong universities follow the US 4.0 model closely, some with a 4.3 maximum for an A+. The number transfers with little adjustment.

countries.name: India (10-point CGPA)
countries.notes: Many Indian universities now issue a 10-point CGPA alongside or instead of a percentage. The often-quoted shortcut of multiplying CGPA by 9.5 converts to a percentage, not to a GPA — running it through as though the result were a US percentage compounds two conversions and gets the answer badly wrong.

countries.name: India
countries.notes: Indian marking is severe by US standards: a First Division starts at 60 and a 75 is a distinction most students never see. Converting an Indian percentage as though it were a US one — 65 becomes a D — is the single commonest error in reading these transcripts, and it is why the division matters more than the number.

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.notes: The Indeks Prestasi Kumulatif runs on a 4.0 scale like the US GPA. The honours labels attached to it (cum laude from 3.51) are set nationally rather than by each university.

countries.name: Iran
countries.notes: Iran marks out of 20 like France, and with the same severity at the top. The undergraduate pass mark is 10, though many programmes require a 12 average to graduate.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.notes: Irish universities use the same honours structure as the UK. Some award a Third-Class Honours between the 2.2 and the Pass; where they do, it sits in the 45-49 range.

countries.name: Israel
countries.notes: Israeli universities mark out of 100 and pass at 60. The distribution sits higher than the British one, so a US-style reading is closer to right here than it is for most of this list.

countries.name: Italy
countries.notes: Italian exam marks run 18 to 30, with 30 e lode above 30 as a distinction. The final degree mark is reported out of 110 instead, with 110 e lode at the top — the two are separate scales and are regularly confused.

countries.name: Japan
countries.notes: Older Japanese transcripts run 優/良/可/不可 with no S grade, in which case 優 is the top mark and maps to an A. The pass mark is 60.

countries.name: Kenya
countries.notes: Kenyan degree classes follow the British model, with the same compression at the top of the percentage range.

countries.name: Malaysia
countries.notes: Malaysian universities use a 4.0 CGPA alongside a First/Second Class honours classification inherited from the British system.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.notes: Mexican universities mark out of 10 and pass at 6, though some private institutions and graduate programmes set the pass at 7 or 8.

countries.name: Nepal
countries.notes: Tribhuvan University's division boundaries are the ones most Nepali transcripts follow. Newer institutions increasingly issue a 4.0 GPA instead.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.notes: The top of the Dutch scale is effectively unused: a 9 is rare and a 10 almost unheard of, so the practical range runs 6 to 8. Treating an 8/10 as 80% and therefore a B badly understates it — an 8 is an excellent Dutch grade.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.notes: The letters look American but the bands are stricter: a New Zealand A starts at 85 where a US A commonly starts at 93 on a 100-point course but is awarded far more often.

countries.name: Nigeria
countries.notes: Nigerian universities use a 5.0 CGPA with British-style honours classes on top. The class is the part US admissions offices read; rescaling the CGPA to 4.0 arithmetically loses the classification, which is the more meaningful signal.

countries.name: Norway
countries.notes: Norway's A-F scale is defined nationally with C as the expected average — deliberately, unlike the US where B has drifted into that role. A Norwegian C is a solid result, not a weak one.

countries.name: Pakistan
countries.notes: Pakistani universities mark on the same compressed scale as India's. Many now issue a 4.0 CGPA as well, which maps to a US GPA far more directly than the percentage does.

countries.name: Peru
countries.notes: Peru marks out of 20 with a pass at 11 — one point higher than the French and Portuguese scales it otherwise resembles.

countries.name: Philippines
countries.notes: The Philippine scale is inverted: 1.00 is the highest mark and 5.00 is a failure. A Filipino student with a 1.25 average has near-perfect marks, and reading it as a 1.25 US GPA — which would be a D average — is the single most damaging misreading on this list.

countries.name: Poland
countries.notes: The Polish scale starts at 2, not 0, and 2 is the failing grade — the usable range is only 3 to 5, which makes proportional scaling meaningless.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.notes: Portugal marks out of 20 and passes at 10, like France, but awards the top of the range rather more readily.

countries.name: Romania
countries.notes: Romania marks out of 10 and passes at 5. Unlike the Dutch scale, the top of the Romanian range is used, so a 10 does appear.

countries.name: Russia
countries.notes: The Russian scale has only three passing grades, so a US 4.0 equivalent is unusually coarse here. A diploma with honours (красный диплом) is the signal that carries the most weight in a US application.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
countries.notes: Saudi universities use either a 5.0 or a 4.0 scale and the transcript states which. Submitting a 5.0-scale figure as though it were out of 4.0 makes a strong record look impossible, so check first.

countries.name: Singapore
countries.notes: NUS and NTU use a 5.0 Cumulative Average Point; SMU uses a 4.0 GPA that transfers directly. Check which scale the transcript states before converting — the two are commonly confused.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.notes: South African universities mark on the British model, so the same compression at the top applies: a 75 is a distinction, not a bare pass.

countries.name: South Korea
countries.notes: Korean universities mostly use a 4.5 maximum, though a few use 4.3 and a few 4.0 — the transcript states which. Dividing a 4.5-scale GPA by 4.5 and multiplying by 4.0 is the usual shortcut, and it systematically understates strong students because the Korean curve is not linear.

countries.name: Spain
countries.notes: Spanish marking is compressed at the top in the same way as the French and Dutch: a Notable is a strong result and Matrícula de Honor is capped at a small percentage of each class by regulation.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
countries.notes: Sri Lankan degree classes follow the British pattern, and the same top-end compression applies.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.notes: Many Swedish courses are graded only Underkänd / Godkänd / Väl godkänd — fail, pass, pass with distinction — with no finer gradation. A transcript of pass grades carries no GPA information at all, and US schools generally accept that.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.notes: Switzerland runs the opposite way to Germany despite the shared language: 6 is the best grade and 4 is the pass mark. A Swiss 4.0 is a bare pass, not the perfect score the same number means in the US.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.notes: Undergraduate courses pass at 60; graduate courses usually pass at 70. Many Taiwanese transcripts print a 4.0 GPA alongside the percentage.

countries.name: Thailand
countries.notes: Thai universities grade on a 4.0 scale that mirrors the US one, so the figure carries over almost unchanged.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.notes: Turkish universities grade on a 4.0 scale with letter pairs (AA, BA, BB…) rather than single letters, so the number transfers directly. The graduation threshold is a 2.00 cumulative average.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.notes: Ukrainian universities issue both the traditional 5-point grade and a 100-point ECTS score. Where the transcript carries the ECTS letter, that converts more precisely than the 5-point figure.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.notes: British marking is compressed at the top: a mark above 80 is rare in the humanities and a First is awarded from 70. Applying a US curve to a British transcript is the commonest way a strong UK degree is undersold, which is why most US graduate schools read the classification rather than the percentage.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.notes: Vietnamese universities now issue a 4.0 GPA alongside the 10-point average. Where both appear on the transcript, the 4.0 figure is the one to submit.
